citations.review_text:
This is one of the most boring games I have ever played. I see potential with the style but genuinely it just fails in almost every way possible. Some of the worst and most limited exploration that exists in the "Open World Survival Craft" genre, really boring and rough on the eyes UI, tutorial is borderline useless and wastes your time only telling you things that are already extremely obvious while failing to teach helpful mechanics/tips, the combat is extremely boring as well as the enemy design at least in the starting area and first couple portals, the character customization and skill tree are very limited in options, inventory management is really annoying with the amount of items/resources you randomly can collect early on, building is really boring and felt very limited, and there's just so many issues it would take forever to list. 

It's mind blowing that this game is rated 96% positive at the time of my review because it is 35 USD. I can find 100s of games that are better for that price point. If this game was completely free it would still have been so disappointing that I would not give a positive review, but at least it would be close. I am trying hard to give it a chance and explore what's here but it is actually painfully boring. Please look up a gameplay video before buying if you are tempted just because of how high the positive ratings are. I respect the effort and direction, but the price point and current reviews are so wildly far off from where it should be. I have seen worse games but for this price it's definitely a top contender for worst value.

[b](btw this game requires a modern and beefy PC, so absolutely check the System Requirements tab)[/b]

I really want to like this game, but it's just too tedious. I don't know if it gets more interesting or if it's more fun in multiplayer, but singleplayer definitely plays like a chore. The game often gives you large "remember that resource that was very difficult but mostly tedious to get? Yeah, you now need to grind out ten of them."

The UI is awful, the voice acting is all over the place, and the story is very confusing and difficult to follow. It's silly at first, but definitely not after 34.99$ and knowing that the game is "v1.x."

I absolutely loathe giving indie games negative reviews, but I just can't recommend Abiotic Factor.

claims.claim: Reviewers report experiencing technical issues or bugs during gameplay.

citations.review_text: Abiotic has tons of bugs that are difficult to ignore. I've experienced several gamebreaking ones. Game isn't what it seems and is poorly made. Most mechanics are designed to drain time and cheap grind. Overpriced and built to spam DLC's.

This game is special. It follows the typical survival-crafting game formula, but the setting and premise are unique enough to make it feel fresh. I'm also a sucker for SCP, Control, and Half-life style stories/worlds, so that was a plus. This game takes a sillier approach than those other titles, which is to its benefit. In terms of gameplay, combat is simple yet very enjoyable, as well as pretty intuitive. Ranged combat takes a second to figure out, but it clicked pretty fast for me. Crafting has not felt tedious, and I appreciate how you can craft so many of the basic components, which saves a lot of time that would be spent looking for items in other games. The minigames are also fun. The game can be a bit jank at times, but it never got to the point that the game was unplayable. The story and progression was also a welcome addition, as it removes the aimlessness that can affect more sandbox-style games. Characters are amusing and memorable, and though they don't serve too much function except as guides, the flavor they brought added to the game's quality. Overall, if you're looking for an engaging survival game to play with friends (which is the way you should play), then I highly recommend this one.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the setting and aesthetic as drawing inspiration from Half-Life and SCP-style lore.

citations.review_text: For context, I played and platinumed this game on PS5 and plan to do a PC run, as my first 100 hours in Abiotic Factor were not enough. There are few games that keeps my attention and rob me of my time like this game has and it's easily become one of my Top 10 games of all time. Everything from the survival crafting to the old school Half Life graphics had me hooked. It never felt like the grinding and material farming was too much. The progression of the story and crafting tiers was very balanced and I never felt like specific areas kept me away for too long. I really hope this game keeps getting bigger and far more ridiculous because this game absolutely deserves it.

Abiotic Factor is a science themed survival crafting game, that leaves you with the need to explore every nook & cranny and discover the crazy story behind the GATE Cascade Research Facility and its experiments! - PSA: Remember if you "See it, Report it" - Shout out to you all at Deep Field Games! cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: Mid-game survivors engage with extensive base building using office appliances, though combat encounters introduce massive health pools and sudden damage.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that late-game enemies possess massive health pools, making combat feel tedious or like a whackfest

citations.review_text:
As much as I loved the game, and I'm writing this just as I finished the game with my girlfriend, I can't just recommend it without addressing some major design decisions that made the game almost unbearable before the ending.

I can almost certainly say that the game has some "Dark Souls second half" syndrome. While we had a blast during the first half (considering the hydroplant as a mid-game delimitator), during the second half we found ourselves thinking "omfg, all of this again??" and just hoping for the story to continue. The game is just... too repetitive. It worked, a lot, but I feel the developers dragged it out for too long and it kind of lost the magic, to the point that whenever I found a button, even before pressing it I knew "this button won't work" and we'd have to go on yet another crafting journey just to press the f***ing button.

Not even mentioning the unholy health pools enemies have near the end, to the point that I had to turn on KeepInventory and reduce enemy health so my girlfriend could have a nice time. Firearm enemies don't have any sort of anticipation either, they just shoot you the nanosecond they see you, so you take bullets feeling like it was unfair (which is a REAAAAAALLY bad indicator for game designers), and that turned into a huge pain in the ass when you had those "fixed machine gun" moments. Oh, and decay rates for food stacks are shared... not by item, if you place fresh meat on an almost-rotting stack, it will rot along with the rest.... ouch.

Abiotic Factor is a survival crafting game with a unique aesthetic that can get a bit grindy at times, but was a pretty fun experience overall, especially with friends!

The main pull for Abiotic Factor is definitely its aesthetic, which I've never seen in a survival crafting game like this. You play as scientists in a half-life inspired laboratory complex, where you have to scavenge office supplies, lab equipment, and visit alien worlds to get the materials needed to expand your base and arsenal and defend yourself against the hostile forces attacking the complex, while trying to find a way out yourself. It feels very unique and adds a fun variation on the usual forest/cave environments you usually find yourself exploring in these kinds of games.

The combat is a bit basic, which is fine at the start and you can definitely unlock some cool weapons later on, but there's not much interaction beyond slashing, shooting, and shielding. Especially when enemies get (much) tougher later in the game it sometimes feels like a bit of a whackfest and just hoping they will die before you do. Special shout-out to the final boss fight which felt pretty much incomprehensible, and didn't even have any stakes because we could just respawn directly into it whenever we died. Even after having defeated it, I'm still not sure how we actually did it to be honest.

The other main issue with Abiotic Factor is getting around the map and gathering materials. Various components for your recipes will be available only in specific areas in the complex, so you'll sometimes have to travel quite a bit to gather these. Although there are vehicles and a tram-system, these always feel a little sub-optimal and still take quite some travel time, especially compared to a more sandbox game where you can design this kind of transport method yourself. This travel time is also worsened by the fact that materials in the complex itself do not respawn, once you use them, they're gone for good! Materials only r…

Super fun game, and highly recommend to play with friends or online!
I really like the story and all the exploration, but the only thing I didn't like was how difficult the main enemies are near the end of the story, but there are optional settings to lower Enemy HP to combat it, otherwise the game is great!

While we had a blast during the first half (considering the hydroplant as a mid-game delimitator), during the second half we found ourselves thinking "omfg, all of this again??" and just hoping for the story to continue. The game is just... too repetitive. Not even mentioning the unholy health pools enemies have near the end, to the point that I had to turn on KeepInventory and reduce enemy health so my girlfriend could have a nice time. Firearm enemies don't have any sort of anticipation either, they just shoot you the nanosecond they see you, so you take bullets feeling like it was unfair (which is a REAAAAAALLY bad indicator for game designers), and that turned into a huge pain in the ass when you had those "fixed machine gun" moments. Oh, and decay rates for food stacks are shared... not by item, if you place fresh meat on an almost-rotting stack, it will rot along with the rest.... ouch.

My first review of Abiotic Factor was pretty negative, but after giving it a second chance, I think I understand why my experience was so mixed.

One of the biggest issues I had (and still sometimes have) is progression. The game loves hiding the path forward behind vents, side rooms, key items, or objectives that are easy to miss. There were multiple points where I felt like I had thoroughly explored an area, only to discover later that I had overlooked a single vent or doorway that was required to continue. I don't like relying on guides, so getting stuck and wandering around trying to figure out where to go next could be pretty frustrating.

My first playthrough was as a duo, and we eventually made it to the Labs before calling it quits. We weren't really enjoying ourselves by that point and decided to stop.

My second playthrough has been with a group of four, and the experience has been significantly better. Exploring, building, gathering resources, and dealing with threats is much more enjoyable when there's a larger group working together. Even with three completely new players, we're having a lot of fun overall.

That said, there are still moments where enemy damage or certain encounters feel overtuned. Every now and then something hits absurdly hard and the reaction is basically, "Okay, that wasn't very fun." It's not enough to ruin the experience, but it does create some frustrating spikes.

Despite those complaints, my opinion of the game has improved a lot. Abiotic Factor shines when you're playing with friends and embracing the chaos of surviving a science facility gone horribly wrong. The atmosphere, crafting, and cooperative gameplay are excellent. I just wish the game did a slightly better job of nudging players in the right direction when they've missed a critical path forward.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game incorporates base building mechanics that allow players to repurpose office furniture, equipment, and appliances found throughout the facility

citations.review_text:
Abiotic factor combines two of my favorite things: Original Half life and SCP. A game where you play in a Black Mesa like facility as a scientist after a security breach. There are solgers clearing the facility out, anomalies and creatures who escaped, and portals into other dimensions. Pretty much the recipe for a chaotic, fun and clever multiplayer experience.  I can’t even imagine the chaos with 6 other fellow scientists.
The game is made with incredibly a lot of love. Filled with references, jokes and crossovers. I found myself reading every e-mail, listening to every line of dialogue, and appreciating all the little details that made the facility as charming as it is. The game is incredibly immersive in my opinion.

The map is one massive interconnected facility. I got lost all the time, my friend was laughing at my poor sense of direction. 10/10. There is environmental story telling as you progress in the story, with enemies’ spawns and such. 
The base building is great. You re use the furniture and cabinets from around the facility to build your base. You can as well craft barricades, traps, shelfs, etc. You pick a corner to make your home, it will be messy, minimalistic, and absolutely an OSHA violation. I love that you can just infinitely stack boxes, what lead to an insane storage system. Your base needs power. How do you supply it? Obviously, you connect plugboard into another plugboard until the whole base is a fire hazard, ready to break any moment. But that is how science works right? 

We went in completely blind, not even knowing how long the game takes to complete. Every time it felt like the final area, we got send to a new place. I am pleasantly surprised by the length of the game. I must say some areas feel a bit emptier, but so many are just amazing to be in. 

The game has few crossovers like one with “voices of the void” amazing side area for you to explore. And Core Keeper (what is one of my all-time favorite games). I felt like I am hallucin…

Abiotic Factor is basically what happens when a bunch of scientists get trapped in a giant underground facility and immediately decide that stealing every chair, microwave and filing cabinet is the key to survival.

Exploration is great, building and crafting are genuinely fun, and playing it with friends makes the whole thing ten times better. The atmosphere is somehow creepy, cozy and hilarious at the same time.

One of the best co-op survival games I’ve played in a long time. Highly recommended.

A gem which apparently somehow nobody ever talks about (except two unrelated middle-aged trans women in our entourage. thank you for your service and impeccable taste and pointing it out to me)

So invested in it that it's hard to think about other things, no idea how far we are into the game, and just hoping it'll keep going on. 
It brilliantly nails its clear inspirations while remaining uniquely rich with its very own vibe, and you never stop unlocking new shortcuts to interconnect the whole world filled to the brim with secrets. It's a sleepover at an equivalent of Black Mesa during the resonance cascade failure between interdimensional worlds, in which you can have a blatant disregard for SCP containment, because this dangerously physics-breaking anomaly would look great in your cosy little nest entirely built in your crumbling workplace from an "abusive use of office furniture" - in which you can hear the occasional distant screams of your scientist colleagues getting murdered by unidentified entities, with a coworker occasionally showing up on all four at your door begging for some food scraps and coffee. 
You can totally prank your friends by not telling them that the new sofa you've installed in the living room, was retrieved from a reinforced containment cell with a redacted file forbidding anyone to approach it. Surely this will make some harmless fun !

Totally soloable while also playable up to 6 friends if you have such a number of those, (though if you're solo please do build those wheeled carts to amass more ressources at once they're so so handy) and with lots of options of accessibility in case you could be not fond of some survival mechanics or want to limit stress and focus on the discoveries and story or homemaking in peace. It's good survival stuff tho. 
You can switch your game to solo/multiplayer anytime also ! (but the custom server options May possibly be reset when you do that, so just check to be sure they're still how you had left them)
…

The map in this game is probably the best I've ever seen, beautifully intertwining around itself. You simply can't draw maps of these places because they use the 3D space so well. You will get lost at times, but eventually you get familiar with the turns and routes around. Every time I go back somewhere old, I'll find a new path with a secret room or area, which can give you rare drops or unique furniture. Deciding where to build your base is a lot of fun, since anywhere with a plug socket is technically a candidate, and there are hundreds of those. And it's so satisfying when you unlock a shortcut door that leads back to an earlier area. 

The tone of the game is the perfect balance of humour with an ominous overlay. It works perfectly in multiplayer. I don't even normally care for crafting in games, but the advantage of having to make something complicated is you get to go back through the map looking for the ingredients. Definitely give this game a try - it has something for everyone, not just the map lovers.

what a game. so many creative ways to get around the facility, tons of options for backtracking. a really fun game to just navigate. you'll find yourself knowing the place like the back of your hand before you even realize. i find myself dreaming of how to move stuff back to my base before bed. good stuff.

citations.review_text:
Quite possibly one of the greatest games to release in 2025 and one of the best survival crafting games to date.

Varied and interesting locations, lots of things to craft, base building that you can do almost anywhere if you have the resources and balls for it, many different enemies and entities to overcome, plenty of customisation in both character and gameplay settings to tailor your own personal experience (such as stack sizes) all within an atmosphere that calls back to the original Half Life.

It's just really interesting and doesn't try to be anything that it isn't. The linear progression works, it's not trying to be Valheim or Minecraft or anything else along those lines with a huge expansive world to explore. If that's not your thing, that's fine. But I think it works really well.

It's genuinely a lot of fun, and I cannot wait for the DLC to release.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that world settings can be customized to adjust stack sizes and experience multipliers.

citations.review_text: Having been around for most of it's early access, Abiotic Factor made it's way rather easily into my favorite games. It has a blend of features I like, such as a trait system akin to Project Zomboid, a way to customize your experince which is good if you hate grind and inventory management (you can increase stack sizes to 30 times what they are by default), But the gameplay itself has a degree of crafting and survival in a sort of Black Mesa type facility like Half-Life crossed with the SCP Foundation. Portals are both how you get renewable resources, as they reset every few in game days, and generally advance the game, as there is usually something in each portal you need that you can only really get from there at that part of the game. As you progress you unlock new things, and while the game feels a bit "undercooked" to me by the time you get close to the end, with enemies taking way too much effort to kill, the developers are still actively patching and updating the game, so that is likely to be ironed out over time as the game keeps receiving polish. However a review has to be based on what "is" not what can be, and what is currently in the game is worth the asking price. Despite using unreal engine 5, the game still actually runs relatively decently on my ancient potato of a PC.

Bought this game knowing absolutely nothing about it, and it turned out to be one of my favorite games of all time! It activated my gamer brain. Being creative with the environment feels so rewarding, and you can straight-up "cheat" your way through a lot of areas if you think outside the box. The game doesn't spoon-feed you everything, it guides you naturally through environmental storytelling, NPC dialogues, and reading emails. Paying attention and actually figuring things out on your own is one of the best experiences you can get here.

Since it's a sandbox game, you can always adjust your world to suit your play style. Hate inventory management? Increase the item stack size. Playing solo? Increase the EXP multiplier so the EXP grinding doesn't feel too tedious!

I highly recommend playing alone first if you want to get the true experience of discovering stuff. I love everything about this game, the level design, the story, the setting, and the general vibe. Everything is just perfect.
